# Truehound docs

> Truehound is the AI access agent that proves its work: it finds the accounts people, service accounts and AI agents hold across connected apps, removes them with a person's approval, and re-reads each app to prove they are gone.

# Getting started

Source: https://truehound.io/docs/getting-started/
Last compared with the product's code: 2026-10-25

Truehound is an AI access agent. It finds who has access to your apps, removes what should be gone, and proves each removal by reading the app again. Start by looking at your own GitHub organization for nothing, or open the demo, then connect your apps and run one review.

**What you need, and what is not on yet.** The free scan and the live demo need no account. Everything else needs a Truehound workspace on a plan. Email sign-in links are not switched on yet: you sign in by payment, an activation code, an invite link or a passkey.

## Try it before you buy

There are two ways in that ask for nothing. Neither one needs an account.

- The [free scan](https://truehound.io/scan/) reads your GitHub organization with a token you create. It shows the real score and counts, with names hidden, and finds former staff, outside admins, old deploy keys, public repos and secrets in code.
- The [live demo](https://truehound.io/demo/) is the whole product on a made-up company. Nothing you do in it touches a real app. There are also [click-through tours](https://truehound.io/tours/), one per task.

## Set up in this order

1. **Open a workspace**
   Pick a plan on the [pricing page](https://truehound.io/pricing/). The price is flat and never per seat. After you pay, the page Stripe returns you to signs you in.
   A teammate joins by an invite link from an admin. Later, a passkey saved on your device signs you back in.

2. **Connect your identity source and your HR system**
   Connect the system that says who is a current employee first. Truehound takes the leaving date from your HR system when you have one, and uses your identity provider to confirm it. If a person is suspended in the identity provider but still active in other apps, that is a finding.
   See [Connect your apps](https://truehound.io/docs/connect-apps/) for each way an app can be connected.

3. **Connect the apps that hold your data**
   Add your code host, cloud accounts and the apps your team uses. Each app has a card on the Sources page that says what Truehound can read, whether it can remove people through that app's own API, and which plan the vendor needs for that.

4. **Read the people list and the Left, still has access board**
   People shows one row per person across every app, with each account, role and last sign-in. Accounts that match no person are listed under No person for you to resolve.
   The Left, still has access board lists everyone who has left and still holds an active account somewhere, worst first, with a clock from the day they left.

5. **Run your first review and keep the proof**
   Start an [access review](https://truehound.io/docs/access-reviews/), decide every line, sign off, and download the evidence pack. Each change is sealed in Proof, a hash chain you can verify yourself.

## Where things live

- Sources: connect, reconnect and check each app.
- People and Left, still has access: who holds what, and who should not.
- Access review and Review campaigns: run, schedule and sign off reviews.
- Access requests and Joiners and leavers: self-serve access, and the offboarding runs.
- Autopilot: the AI jobs and their switches.
- AI keys and agents: the AI keys and agents people created, and MCP hooks.
- Proof: every action, verifiable.
- Settings: your Anthropic key, roles, approvals and the developer tools.

## What Truehound will not do

- It never calls someone departed unless you list them or your HR system or identity provider says so.
- It never shows a check it could not run as a pass. Apps it could not read are listed as not checked, with the reason.
- It counts a removal as done only when it has read the app again and the access is gone. A removal you did by hand is labelled manual and is not counted as verified.

---

# Connect your apps

Source: https://truehound.io/docs/connect-apps/
Last compared with the product's code: 2026-10-25

Every app on Sources is connected one of six ways. The card for an app tells you which, what Truehound reads from it, whether it can remove a person through the app's own API, and what plan the vendor requires for that. The [integrations directory](https://truehound.io/apps/) has a page for each app.

**What you need, and what is not on yet.** Which apps you can connect is listed on the integrations page, which counts only apps that are tested and switched on in the live build. Google Workspace and Microsoft Entra ID sign-in need Google and Microsoft client IDs that are not set up yet, and their cards say so. AWS needs Truehound's own AWS account on the connector, and its card says it is not set up on our side yet.

## The six ways to connect

- API token: you create a read-only token in the app (the card links to the right page and lists the steps) and paste it. Some apps need several values, such as a client ID and secret, and the card has one field for each.
- Browser sign-in (OAuth): you sign in to Google or Microsoft in your browser and grant read access. No secret is pasted, and the token is short-lived.
- SCIM: for apps that expose a SCIM user list on a plan that includes it, you paste the SCIM bearer token. Truehound reads the users and can deactivate them.
- Browser playbook: for apps with no user API on your plan, an admin stores a dedicated service account's sign-in. A scripted browser reads or removes members, limited to the app's own hosts. A page that has changed stops the run instead of guessing.
- Imported list: for an app with no API at all, you paste its users table, import its CSV, or read it from a screenshot or PDF. The import is the scan, and its file hash is sealed in Proof.
- Custom connector: for your own or niche app, you describe its users endpoint, authentication, paging and field mapping with no code, and it runs on the same engine as the built-in apps.

## Connect an app with a token

1. **Open the app's card on Sources**
   Search by name. The card lists what Truehound reads and the plan the vendor needs.

2. **Create the token where the card points you**
   Use the narrowest scope that reads users. Give a token that can remove people only if you want one-click removal, and only for apps where the card says removal is supported.

3. **Paste it and connect**
   Truehound reads the app once and shows what it found. If the vendor refuses part of the read, that part shows as not checked with the vendor's reason, and is never shown as a pass.

## What each card tells you

- Capability labels: read users, roles, last sign-in, revoke, verify, and which of those need a higher plan at the vendor.
- Whether removal works through the API. Some plans have no removal API at all, and the card says so once.
- Freshness. A review will not start on data that is stale. Imported lists stay fresh for 7 days.
- Plain error words. A refused token says what the vendor said and how to fix it.

## Identity and HR systems

Connect your identity provider (Okta, JumpCloud, Google Workspace or Microsoft Entra ID) and your HR system (for example BambooHR, Rippling, Deel, HiBob, Personio, Gusto, Workday or Kombo). The HR system is the authority on the day a person left. The identity provider corroborates it, and the page shows both dates and the gap when they differ.

Device managers (Jamf Pro, Kandji and Microsoft Intune) tie computers to people and appear on leavers' offboarding. They add devices, not accounts.

## Where your credentials go

Without an account, tokens stay in your browser. With a team workspace, credentials an admin chooses to store for scheduled reads are encrypted on the server and never returned. See [Security and data handling](https://truehound.io/docs/security-data/) for how.

> Apps that need the connector's relay (because the vendor does not answer browsers) forward your token for that request only. The relay does not log it.

---

# Access reviews

Source: https://truehound.io/docs/access-reviews/
Last compared with the product's code: 2026-10-25

An access review asks the right people to keep or remove each account in each app, records why, removes what they decide to remove, checks that it is gone, and gives your auditor a pack they can verify. Truehound builds the list, suggests a decision with a reason on every line, and refuses to sign off while anything is open.

**What you need, and what is not on yet.** Reviews, sign-off and the evidence pack work in a workspace and in the live demo. Recurring schedules that launch on the server need a team workspace. Delivery of reviews inside Slack and Microsoft Teams is built but not switched on yet, because the Slack app and the Teams bot are not registered. Reviewers outside Truehound get a link instead.

## Start a review

1. **Check the scope**
   Before launch you see the population: how many accounts across how many apps, how many are flagged, and who the reviewers will be.
   A freshness gate blocks the launch if an app's data is stale, so a review never freezes old data. Apps that could not be read are listed as not checked.

2. **Launch**
   Launching freezes a snapshot. Later changes in the apps do not move the lines under a reviewer.

## Decide every line

- Each line shows the person, the account, the role, last activity and the source, and the usage band where the app reports one.
- Each line carries a suggested decision with a one-line reason. Without an Anthropic key the suggestion comes from rules and is labelled as rules. With your own key, Claude can write the reasons, and that is an explicit per-workspace opt-in. See [AI keys](https://truehound.io/docs/ai-keys/).
- A reason is required on every decision, keep or revoke. You can keep many lines at once with one comment.
- A reviewer cannot decide their own account. Reviewers can delegate a line with a reason, and an admin can reassign lines in bulk.
- A review can have one to three stages: a manager, an app owner, or named people. Stage two sees stage one's decision and reason.
- Accept a risk with a reason of 20 or more characters, a named owner and an expiry within a year. When it expires the line reopens by itself.
- Usage shown beside each line helps you justify a keep or a revoke.

## Revoke, then verify

A revoke decision removes the access through the app's API under your approval policy, then Truehound reads the app again. The line counts as done only when the re-read agrees. A cancelled dialog records nothing.

If the re-read still sees the account, or could not run, sign-off stays blocked until you try again, remove it by hand, or accept the risk with a written reason.

A removal done by hand carries a note and up to three screenshots or PDFs and a ticket link. They go into the evidence pack unchanged with their hashes. It stays labelled manual and is not counted as verified until a later read shows the account gone.

For privileged access, Truehound can remove every path to it, whether direct, through a group or through a role, and catch access that is inherited. It previews the effect first.

## Sign off

Sign-off is named and carries an attestation. It is refused while any line or revoke is open. Reminders and escalation to the campaign owner are built, but they go out by email, which is not switched on yet.

## Schedule reviews

On Review campaigns, a signed-in workspace saves a recurring review on the server: monthly through annual, or every 1 to 365 days, full or delta (only accounts that are new, or whose roles or admin status changed, since the last run).

The server cron launches each schedule on its date with nobody in the app, once per date. It waits, and says why, while another review is open or no app has been read yet. A schedule can end on its due date and skip or revoke undecided lines, with each revoke going through the approval policy. You can also manage schedules as code with [Terraform](https://truehound.io/docs/terraform/) or the [API](https://truehound.io/docs/api-webhooks/).

## The evidence pack

- A ZIP with a CSV per system, the decisions with reasons, the revocations with their verification state, accepted risks, and escalations.
- A manifest with SHA-256 hashes of every file, so an auditor can check that nothing changed, and a PDF summary.
- A read-only auditor link to one pack, valid 1 to 90 days and revocable. Every view, download and check is logged for you.
- Control mapping to frameworks, and evidence expiry warnings before evidence goes stale.
- Automatic push of the pack to Vanta or Drata when you sign off, once you connect either on the Controls page.
- Every launch, decision, delegation, accepted risk and sign-off is sealed in Proof, which you can verify in the app, in the auditor's browser, or offline with the verifier included in the pack.

> Truehound does not hold a SOC 2 report or any certification. The pack gives your auditor the evidence of your own review.

---

# Offboarding

Source: https://truehound.io/docs/offboarding/
Last compared with the product's code: 2026-10-25

Offboarding in Truehound is one checklist for one person across every connected app. It removes access where an app's API allows, tells you exactly what you must do by hand for the rest, lists the apps it could not check, and ends with a receipt.

**What you need, and what is not on yet.** The Left, still has access board and the offboarding checklist work in a workspace and in the demo. Automatic removal when a leaver's run is approved is off by default and an admin switches it on, and it needs a team workspace. Hand-over of repositories and Drive files is built and needs a team workspace. An HR event opening a run on its own needs your HR system to send the event.

## Find who left

The Left, still has access board lists everyone suspended or deleted in your identity source, or marked as leaving in your HR system, who still holds an active account somewhere. A contractor past their end date counts too. The clock runs from the day they left to the last removal, and the worst case is first.

The leaving date comes from your HR system when you have one, then from your identity provider, so the board and the offboarding page always tell the same story. In the GitHub audit you can also paste the names of people who left, or upload a CSV, and every member and outside collaborator is checked against it.

## Run the offboarding

1. **We can remove**
   Apps where the connection allows removal. One click removes the person, then Truehound reads the app again to prove it held. You can remove every API account in one confirmation.

2. **You remove, we check**
   Apps with no removal API on your plan. The page gives you the admin link and the vendor's steps, you remove the person, and you mark it done. It is labelled manual and is not counted as verified until a later read shows the account gone.

3. **Not checked**
   Apps Truehound could not read are listed with the reason. They are never hidden and never shown as clean.

4. **Finish and keep the receipt**
   The receipt shows apps covered, how many removals were verified and how many were manual, and the time from the day they left. It is sealed in Proof and can be downloaded. A finished run stays as its receipt and is never planned again from scratch.

## Removal on approval

A leaver's run can remove the person through each app's own API when it is approved. An admin switches this on, it is off by default, and the switch is sealed in Proof. The approval shows how many apps it will remove the person from. Removal is verified by a re-read in the same way as in a review. The supported apps each cite the vendor's own documentation for the removal call.

Offboarding playbooks branch by exit type (voluntary, involuntary, contractor), department, title, location and app, with timed steps.

## Start a run from your HR system

An HR termination sent to Truehound by webhook, or an identity provider's SCIM deactivation, opens the person's offboarding run at once. Admins are told, and the run waits for an approval. There is one run per person, and the trigger can be switched off per workspace. You can also start one through the [API](https://truehound.io/docs/api-webhooks/) with a people event or an offboarding request.

## What else is covered

- Devices from Jamf Pro, Kandji and Intune appear on the leaver's page.
- Accounts that belong to no person are shown under No person, with suggestions you can accept, dismiss or snooze, so a leaver's second account is not missed.
- The reasons and the elapsed time feed the leaver reconciliation in the evidence pack, as hours from leaving to removal.

> Slack below the Business+ plan has no removal API. Truehound says so on the card and gives you the manual steps.

---

# Access requests

Source: https://truehound.io/docs/access-requests/
Last compared with the product's code: 2026-10-25

An access request is a short form: which app, which role, why, and for how long. The right person approves or denies with a reason. Truehound grants the access through the app and checks it, or hands the work to the app's owner as a task. Every step is recorded in Proof.

**What you need, and what is not on yet.** Access requests need a team workspace and, for each app, a connection that can grant access. Requests and approvals inside Slack and Microsoft Teams are built but not switched on yet, because the Slack app and the Teams bot are not registered. Email approvals need email sending, which is not on yet. Approving in Truehound works today.

## Make an app requestable

On the Access requests page an admin picks which connected apps people may request, which roles, and who approves: the owner, the manager, or the manager and then the owner. The approval policy sets how many people approve, and an admin role needs more.

An app with no owner says so in plain words, and the request goes to an admin.

## Request, approve, grant

1. **The employee asks**
   They choose the app and role, say why, and say for how long. The request shows the seat cost, any unused seats that could be reused instead, and the department's budget impact.

2. **The approver decides**
   An approver approves or denies in Truehound or through the API. Once the Slack app is registered, they can do it in Slack too. A denial must carry a reason, and the requester sees it. Separation-of-duties rules are enforced at request time.

3. **Truehound grants and checks**
   It grants the access through the app's API, SCIM, or the identity provider's groups, then reads the app again before calling it granted. If the app has no API, the request becomes a task for the owner with evidence.

4. **Time-bound access ends on time**
   Access with an end date counts down. At expiry, the server removes it, restores the role the person had before, and reads the app again. The requester can end it early.

## More ways in

- The employee App hub lists apps people can request and shows their own access and who administers each app.
- Claude, through the [MCP server](https://truehound.io/docs/mcp-hooks/), and the [API](https://truehound.io/docs/api-webhooks/) can list, request, approve, deny and cancel requests as the person whose token is used, under the same approval policy and with the same rule that nobody approves their own request.
- Tasks for an app's owner can be pushed as tickets to Jira or ServiceNow, with field mapping and the ticket kept as evidence.
- When an app has no seats left, the request offers reclaiming an unused one or buying another.

## Let Autopilot handle the routine ones

The Autopilot grant job can approve routine requests inside rules you set, for a set time, and send unusual ones to a person with its reasons. See [Autopilot](https://truehound.io/docs/autopilot/).

---

# Autopilot

Source: https://truehound.io/docs/autopilot/
Last compared with the product's code: 2026-10-25

Autopilot is the AI that does the routine access work, within limits you set and cannot be talked out of. Each of its five jobs is off, prepare for approval, or act alone. Whatever it does is in a log in the first person with its reason, and a change counts as made only when a re-read of the app confirms it.

**What you need, and what is not on yet.** Autopilot runs on the team server, so it needs a team workspace, and it is off until an admin switches it on. It works on rules alone. Claude writes the reasons only when your workspace has added its own Anthropic key and opted in, and every action says which one decided. The live demo shows Autopilot over the demo's sample findings.

## The five jobs

- Triage new findings: gives every new finding a priority (now, today or this week) and the reason. Modes: off or auto. It starts on auto.
- Remove stale and risky access: removes dormant accounts (30 to 365 days without a sign-in, 90 by default), unexpected guests and the agent's detections, in the apps you name, then re-reads each app. At most 1 to 100 accounts per run, 10 by default.
- Grant routine requests: grants requests that fit the approval step's rules for a set time, proves it with a re-read, and removes the access when the time is up. Anything unusual goes to a person with the reasons.
- Pre-fill reviews and chase reviewers: fills every open review line with keep, revoke or a person should look, citing the facts. It chases reviewers who have not answered after 2 days by default and escalates after 5.
- Run leavers end to end: removes a leaver's accounts, re-reads each app, reclaims the seats and records the saving, and files the evidence.

## Off, approve or auto

Approve means Autopilot prepares the change and a person approves it. Auto means it acts alone inside the job's rules. The remove, grant, review and leaver jobs start on approve. Nothing runs until an admin switches Autopilot on. A cron picks up every workspace that has it on and has not stopped it.

## Rules nobody can loosen

- Never an admin role. It never grants one, never pre-fills keep on one, and never removes an admin account alone.
- Never a two-approval policy. Where your approval policy asks for two or more approvals, people approve.
- Never a deny without a person. Autopilot escalates with reasons. Only a person denies a request.
- Everything it reads from apps, tickets and requests is data, never an instruction to it.
- The kill switch stops every job before its next action.

> A setting that would loosen one of these rules is refused by the server, whatever the value.

## The kill switch, the log and undo

- The kill switch is always in reach. It records who pressed it and why, and is checked before every action. Resume is an admin action.
- The live log has one row per action: what it did, in the first person, the reason, who decided (rules, or Claude on your own key, checked against the rules), and the evidence.
- An admin can undo an action where the app allows it. Every action is also one event in Proof.
- The page leads with what it did: changes made, how many a re-read confirmed, what waits for a person, and what was undone.

## How it uses Claude

Claude has no tools in Autopilot. Its answers are checked against the rules before anything acts. Without your own Anthropic key every job runs on rules and says so. See [AI keys](https://truehound.io/docs/ai-keys/) for how to add one and what is sent.

---

# AI keys (bring your own key)

Source: https://truehound.io/docs/ai-keys/
Last compared with the product's code: 2026-10-25

Every AI feature in Truehound runs on your own Anthropic key. An admin pastes the key once, switches AI on, and the charges go to your own Anthropic account. If you never add a key, nothing is sent to Anthropic and everything works from rules.

**What you need, and what is not on yet.** AI is off by default. Truehound has no key of its own for customers, and pays nothing for your AI. Without your key every feature runs its rules and is labelled as rules. The key and the opt-in are per workspace and need a team workspace. Provider inventory of AI keys covers OpenAI, Anthropic and GitHub Copilot.

## Add your Anthropic key

1. **Create a key in your Anthropic account**
   Use a key made for Truehound so you can see its usage and revoke it on its own.

2. **Paste it under Settings, AI**
   Truehound proves the key works with one call that lists models, which costs nothing, then stores it encrypted (AES-256-GCM, under a key derived for your workspace). Only its last four characters are ever shown again.

3. **Opt in**
   A consent screen lists exactly what is sent to Anthropic. One switch turns AI on for every AI use in the workspace. You can turn it off again at any time.

## What it does to your data

- Only the facts a feature needs are sent: for review suggestions, each row's app, name, email, roles, status, last sign-in, and admin, two-step and guest flags. The consent screen lists the rest.
- The key is never in a response, a log, an export or an audit line. You can replace or remove it, and each change is sealed in Proof with who made it and the last four characters, never the key.
- Anthropic's commercial terms bar training on customer content ([Anthropic commercial terms](https://www.anthropic.com/legal/commercial-terms), Customer Content).
- A usage meter shows calls and tokens this month, taken from Anthropic's own responses. There is an hourly rate limit per workspace.

## What turns on

With a key and the opt-in: reasons on review lines, the review and approval step, request decisions inside your rules, guided fixes, the campaign builder, the assistant, scheduled agents, and Claude on [Autopilot](https://truehound.io/docs/autopilot/) and in drafted MCP hook policies.

Without a key, each of those runs its rules, labelled as rules, and the app shows an empty state that tells you to add a key.

## AI keys and agents, the inventory

The AI keys and agents page is a different thing: it is the inventory of AI keys other people created. It reads every AI API key, project, service account and Copilot seat from the providers' admin APIs (OpenAI, Anthropic and GitHub Copilot), with its owner and its last use where the provider reports one.

A revoke there counts only when a fresh read agrees. Beside the keys it shows the AI agents and connections Truehound already sees: MCP servers and agent tokens, sign-ins to AI apps reported by the browser extension, AI bots in connected apps, and OAuth grants to AI apps from Google and Microsoft.

When a person leaves, the agents, tokens and apps they created can be offboarded with them. The live demo shows this page on a fictional company.

## AI spend

Spend by person, team and model, with budgets per workspace and team, a month-end forecast and spike alerts, is on the same page.

---

# MCP hooks and Truehound in Claude

Source: https://truehound.io/docs/mcp-hooks/
Last compared with the product's code: 2026-10-25

Two separate things share the MCP name. An MCP hook runs in your developers' AI clients and asks Truehound allow, ask or deny before each tool call. The MCP server lets Claude and other assistants read your access data and file requests in Truehound, under the same approvals as a person.

**What you need, and what is not on yet.** Both need a team workspace. The hook is an open script that needs Node 18 or newer. Drafting hook policies with Claude needs your own Anthropic key, and without one the drafts come from rules. The endpoint is the address shown on your workspace's Developers page.

## MCP hooks: govern calls without a gateway

A small open script runs in the agent client before each tool call. It sends one small request to your workspace and turns the answer into the client's own hook output. Nothing is rerouted: the tool call still goes from the client straight to the MCP server. Read every line of the script before you install it.

Supported clients: Claude Code, Cursor, Windsurf, VS Code Copilot (preview) and Codex CLI, each through its own documented hook.

## Install the hook

1. **Create a hook token**
   On AI agents, MCP hooks, create a token for the workspace, or one per person so every call is tied to that person. It is shown once.

2. **Run the install command on each laptop**
   The page shows a command for your client that downloads the script and installs it. It reads the token from an environment variable, writes it to a file only the user can read, and adds the hook to the client's user config. Running it again updates it and never adds a second entry.
   For managed laptops, print the client config and deploy it by MDM instead.

Shape of the install command (the page fills in your token and address):

```
curl -fsSL https://truehound.io/hooks/truehound-hook.mjs -o /tmp/truehound-hook.mjs
TRUEHOUND_HOOK_TOKEN=<token> node /tmp/truehound-hook.mjs install --client claude-code --api <address>
```

## What the hook sends, and how it behaves

- A summary of the tool input, at most 2,000 characters, with secrets replaced by [REDACTED] on the laptop first. The server redacts again before it stores anything.
- The request is abandoned after 250 milliseconds. An allow is cached for the time your workspace sets (60 seconds by default), so a repeated call makes no request.
- If Truehound is unreachable, your workspace's fail mode decides. Open, the default, lets the call run and keeps a record to send next time. Closed denies it. A policy can set its own.
- The option for all tools also checks built-in tools such as shell commands. The browser option also checks the client's own web fetch and search, so an agent's browsing is governed by site.

> The hook cannot see a person driving a browser, or an agent that drives a browser with no tool call through the client. The Truehound browser extension does not observe agent browser actions.

## Policies and evidence

- Policies allow, ask or deny by MCP server, tool, user, group or an input pattern, with a monitor mode that records without blocking.
- Every MCP server seen is listed, approved or not (shadow MCP), and you approve one in a click.
- Policies can be drafted from your last 30 days of history, by Claude on your own key or by rules, with each rule's impact before you apply it.
- Every call is kept redacted for the retention you set (365 days by default), measured latency is shown, and the calls export as CSV.

## Truehound in Claude: the MCP server

Truehound serves a remote MCP server (Streamable HTTP, JSON-RPC) at the `/mcp` path of your API address. Anyone in the workspace can make a token for themselves. A token can be read only, and can expire after 1 to 365 days. Claude and other MCP clients can also sign in with OAuth 2.1, with a consent page, short-lived access tokens and refresh tokens that rotate. An admin sets token lifetimes and the client hosts that are allowed.

Tools include who_has_access, find_person, list_leavers, offboard_person, proposal_status, list_access_requests, approve_request, deny_request, cancel_request, review_status, decide_review_rows, start_review, list_unused_licenses, open_ticket and change_role. The Developers page lists every tool and whether it reads or files something.

Writes never change an app directly. A removal or role change files a proposal that people approve under your approval policy, a decision is made as the token's person under the same policy, and nobody can approve their own request. A reviewer decides only their own rows. Every call is sealed in Proof.

---

# API and webhooks

Source: https://truehound.io/docs/api-webhooks/
Last compared with the product's code: 2026-10-25

Everything the app shows about people, accounts, findings, reviews, offboardings, evidence and Proof is available over a REST API, and so are the actions: requesting and approving access, launching and deciding reviews, and starting offboardings. Webhooks tell your systems when something changes.

**What you need, and what is not on yet.** The API, webhooks and SIEM streaming need a team workspace. The address to call is shown on your workspace's Developers page, because the api.truehound.io name is not live yet. The OpenAPI 3.1 file is served at /api/v1/openapi.json on that address, and the [Developers page](https://truehound.io/developers/) renders every operation from it.

## Make an API key

1. **Open Developers in your workspace**
   Choose the scopes the key needs, such as `people:read` or `config:write`.

2. **Copy the key once**
   A key belongs to one workspace. Truehound stores only its hash, so the key is shown a single time. It has the form `th_` followed by an id and a secret.

3. **Call the API**
   Send the key as a Bearer token. A key without the scope an operation needs is refused with 403.

Read your people (use the address your workspace shows):

```
curl <your-api-address>/api/v1/people \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TRUEHOUND_API_KEY"
```

## Basics

- Lists answer { data, next_cursor }. Pass next_cursor back as cursor to get the next page.
- Errors answer { ok: false, error, message }, with the field or scope named in plain words.
- The limit is 600 requests a minute per key.
- Data is what your workspace last published from each app, so it matches what your team sees.
- The API covers people, accounts, systems, findings, leavers, reviews (launch, assign, decide, sign off), offboardings, lifecycle runs, access requests (create, approve, deny, cancel, remind, revoke), evidence, access-path queries, Proof events and verification, review schedules, role bundles, custom roles, the approval policy, separation-of-duties rules, webhooks and SIEM destinations.
- The whole reference, with request and response fields and a curl line for each operation, is on the [Developers page](https://truehound.io/developers/).

## Webhooks

Truehound posts an event to your https endpoint when something changes, once per change. You make an endpoint in Developers or with the API, and its signing secret is shown once. You can rotate it, send a test event, read the delivery log, and send any delivery again.

Events: leaver.detected, review.launched, review.signed, review.ended, revoke.verified, revoke.failed, offboarding.started, offboarding.completed, finding.created, finding.resolved, source.connected, proof.sealed, access.requested, access.approved, access.denied, access.granted, access.revoked, lifecycle.run_planned, lifecycle.run_completed, person.changed and ping.

## Check the signature

Every request carries a Truehound-Signature header of the form t=unix-seconds,v1=signature, where the signature is the HMAC-SHA256 of the text t, a dot, and the raw body, keyed with your endpoint secret. Check it against the raw body before you parse it, and reject requests whose timestamp is more than five minutes old.

Answer with any 2xx status within 10 seconds. Anything else is retried after 1 minute, 5 minutes, 30 minutes, 2 hours, 8 hours and 24 hours, and every attempt is in the delivery log.

Verify a delivery (Node):

```
import crypto from "node:crypto";
export function verifyTruehound(raw, header, secret, toleranceSec = 300) {
  const parts = Object.fromEntries(header.split(",").map((p) => p.split("=")));
  const expected = crypto.createHmac("sha256", secret).update(`${parts.t}.${raw}`).digest("hex");
  const fresh = Math.abs(Date.now() / 1000 - Number(parts.t)) <= toleranceSec;
  return fresh && crypto.timingSafeEqual(Buffer.from(expected), Buffer.from(parts.v1 ?? ""));
}
```

## Stream Proof to your SIEM

Proof can be streamed as OCSF to an S3 bucket, Splunk HEC, Datadog or a signed webhook, set up as SIEM destinations in Developers or over the API. Each destination has a test and a delivery log. The export of every admin action is also available as a file.

## Also for developers

- Manage schedules, the approval policy, role bundles and webhooks as code with the [Terraform provider](https://truehound.io/docs/terraform/).
- Let Claude and other assistants work with your workspace through the [MCP server](https://truehound.io/docs/mcp-hooks/).
- Sign people in to Truehound with SAML 2.0 or OIDC on email domains you prove you own, with roles from your IdP groups, and provision them with [SCIM](https://truehound.io/docs/scim/).
- Add an app Truehound does not have with the no-code custom connector described in [Connect your apps](https://truehound.io/docs/connect-apps/).

# Terraform provider

Source: https://truehound.io/docs/terraform/
Last compared with the product's code: 2026-10-25

Review schedules, the approval policy, role bundles and webhooks are the parts of a Truehound workspace that belong in code review. The provider manages them through the public API, so a change to who approves a fix goes through a pull request like any other change.

**What you need, and what is not on yet.** The provider is not on the Terraform Registry yet, so you cannot install it with a plain terraform init today. It has been applied against the production API, and a second plan found no drift. For a build of the provider, email truehoundhq@truehound.io. It needs a team workspace and an API key.

## What it manages

- truehound_review_schedule: a recurring access review, with cadence, systems, reviewers, due days, full or delta mode, and what happens at the due date.
- truehound_approval_policy: the one approval policy per workspace. Destroying it resets the default.
- truehound_role_bundle: a named set of system and role grants.
- truehound_webhook: a signed webhook endpoint. The signing secret is kept in state as a sensitive value.
- truehound_webhook_events (data source): every webhook event type.

## Configure it

1. **Make an API key**
   In Developers, API keys, make a key with the config:read, config:write, webhooks:read and webhooks:write scopes. See [API and webhooks](https://truehound.io/docs/api-webhooks/).

2. **Point the provider at your workspace**
   Set TRUEHOUND_API_KEY, and TRUEHOUND_ENDPOINT to the API address your workspace shows. The provider defaults to api.truehound.io, which is not live yet.

A quarterly review as code:

```
resource "truehound_review_schedule" "quarterly" {
  name          = "Quarterly SOC 2 access review"
  cadence       = "quarterly"
  start_date    = "2026-11-01"
  systems       = ["slack", "okta", "github"]
  reviewer_mode = "named"
  reviewers     = ["ana@example.com", "lee@example.com"]
  due_days      = 14
}
```

## Drift and import

Terraform reads each object back from the API, so a change made in the app shows as drift in the next plan. Existing schedules, roles and webhooks can be imported. A schedule that Terraform manages is launched by the same server cron as one made in the app.

Change history on every configuration object shows who changed it and when.

> The provider creates and deletes real objects and can reset the approval policy. Try it in a test workspace first.

---

# SCIM

Source: https://truehound.io/docs/scim/
Last compared with the product's code: 2026-10-25

SCIM is used in four different ways in Truehound. They are separate features, and you can use any one without the others.

**What you need, and what is not on yet.** SCIM needs a team workspace. Truehound's SCIM client covers a fixed set of apps (listed below), not every SCIM app, and the SCIM bridge is self-serve, not a managed service. Both take effect only with the apps' own plans that allow SCIM.

## 1. Your identity provider provisions people into Truehound

Truehound is a SCIM 2.0 server (RFC 7643 and 7644). Okta, Microsoft Entra ID, JumpCloud or OneLogin push users to it, with the base path `/api/scim/v2` on your API address and a bearer token that Setup shows once.

The provider's pushes drive the lifecycle. A new user runs your joiner steps, a new department or title runs the mover steps, and a deactivation puts the person on the Left, still has access board and opens their offboarding for approval. Users are created, replaced, patched and deleted, and groups are supported.

Pushed groups map to Truehound roles for Okta (Push Groups) and Entra (group assignment). A user gets the highest role mapped to one of their groups, otherwise the roles attribute, otherwise member. An owner is never changed. Every write is sealed in Proof.

## 2. Truehound provisions and deactivates people in apps

Over SCIM, Truehound can create a user with a role or group, change the role, and deactivate the user, then read the app again to prove each change. The apps with SCIM provisioning built in are Figma, Slack, Atlassian, Notion and Zoom, and Miro, monday.com and Canva for removal.

Slack needs a plan that includes SCIM. Provisioning and removal run under your approval policy.

## 3. Truehound reads an app through its SCIM endpoint

For apps that expose SCIM on a plan that includes it, you paste the SCIM bearer token on the app's card. Truehound reads the user list and can deactivate users. Each app is tested against its documented responses. The integrations directory marks which apps connect this way.

## 4. The SCIM bridge: SCIM for an app that has none

On the SCIM bridge page an admin makes a SCIM 2.0 endpoint for an app that has no SCIM. Behind it is the app's API, through a custom connector, or a browser playbook. It has its own bearer token, shown once, and its path is `/api/scim-bridge/<id>/v2` on your API address.

Your identity provider then deprovisions people in that app like in any SCIM app. A deactivation uses the app's own call, then Truehound reads the app again. The identity provider gets success only when that read agrees.

Okta's PATCH, Entra's string booleans and DELETE all deactivate. Creating a user works only when you set a create call on a custom connector. Attribute changes other than deactivation, and groups, are not written to the app. Every call is listed and sealed in Proof without a body or credential.

## SSO into Truehound is separate

Signing people in to Truehound uses SAML 2.0 or OIDC per workspace, on email domains you prove you own, and is set up under Developers. See [API and webhooks](https://truehound.io/docs/api-webhooks/).

---

# Security and data handling

Source: https://truehound.io/docs/security-data/
Last compared with the product's code: 2026-10-25

Truehound reads people, accounts, roles, status, dates and grants from the apps you connect. It never reads message, document or email bodies. Without an account, what you connect stays in your browser. With a team workspace, the workspace is kept in Cloudflare D1 and every change is sealed in Proof.

**What you need, and what is not on yet.** This page summarizes the [Trust Center](https://truehound.io/trust-center/), which is the full statement and lists what is in place, what is partly in place and what is not yet. Truehound has no SOC 2 report, does not hold ISO 27001 and has had no independent penetration test yet.

## What Truehound reads, and what it never reads

- From connected apps: people, accounts, roles, status, dates and grants.
- Never the content of messages, documents or emails. Mailbox discovery is limited to the sender, subject and date.
- Secret values found in code are masked and never kept.
- Apps it could not read are listed as not checked. They are never shown as clean.

## Where your data lives

Without an account, the token, the audit and the workspace are stored in your browser, not on our servers. The token goes to the vendor, and through our connector only for apps that do not answer browsers or for GitHub code search. The connector relays it per request and does not store or log it.

With a team workspace, the workspace lives in Cloudflare D1. The website is static files on GitHub Pages with no server code. The connector and account backend are a Cloudflare Worker. We run no servers of our own. Every account query is limited to the workspace it belongs to, and automated tests check that a non-member gets not found.

## How credentials are protected

- App credentials an admin chooses to store, including sign-ins for browser playbooks, are encrypted with AES-256-GCM under a key derived for each workspace from a master secret held only in the connector's secret store, and are bound to their workspace and app. The master key can be rotated. They are never returned to the browser.
- Sign-in links, sessions, invites, API keys and extension keys are stored only as SHA-256 hashes. An API key is shown once.
- Your Anthropic key is stored the same way and only its last four characters are ever shown. See [AI keys](https://truehound.io/docs/ai-keys/).
- Truehound has no passwords. You sign in by payment, an activation code, an invite link or a passkey, and the session cookie is HttpOnly and Secure.

## Control over changes

- Owner, admin and member roles, with custom roles and per-area read, edit and act permissions, limit who can change what.
- An approval policy can require one or more approvals, including a second admin, before a fix runs. The person who proposed a fix can never approve it.
- Every change, approval and consent in a workspace is written to Proof, a SHA-256 hash chain where tampering shows. You can verify it in the app and offline, and stream it to your SIEM.
- Autopilot's fixed rules and kill switch limit what automation can do. See [Autopilot](https://truehound.io/docs/autopilot/).

## How long data is kept

An owner can export everything a workspace holds as one JSON file, and can delete the workspace and everything stored for it in one step. A person can delete their own account. A privacy request is answered within 30 days, and customers are told of a personal data breach within 72 hours.

- Sign-in links work for 15 minutes and their records are deleted after 24 hours. A session lasts 30 days from your last visit.
- Scan history is kept 90 days, and the latest successful scan is always kept. Connected-app scans follow the same rule.
- Review links for reviewers outside Truehound expire 120 days after they are made. Invites expire after 7 days.
- Browser-extension sign-in sightings are kept 395 days. Demo-form leads are kept 24 months.
- Restore copies of account data expire within 30 days.

## What we do not have yet

- No SOC 2 report, and no ISO 27001. We do not claim either and will not until an independent auditor issues one.
- No independent penetration test yet.
- Backups are automatic, but we have not yet practised a restore. There is no uptime commitment unless an order form gives one.
- One person, the founder, can reach production.

> The Trust Center has the plan for each gap. Security questionnaires are answered directly, usually within 5 business days, at truehoundhq@truehound.io.

## Also published

- [Sub-processors](https://truehound.io/subprocessors/), with 30 days' notice before one is added or replaced.
- The Data Processing Agreement, Master Service Agreement and service levels under [Legal](https://truehound.io/legal/dpa/).
- A responsible disclosure policy with safe harbour, acknowledgement within 1 business day, and fix targets of 14 days for critical and 30 days for high issues: [security disclosure](https://truehound.io/security-disclosure/).
- The [accessibility conformance report](https://truehound.io/accessibility/) and the public [status page](https://truehound.io/system-status/).
